title: Strings
summary: A string is a character array, and an edit often copies.

parts.rule: Treat a string as a character sequence with array-like indexing, then ask whether an edit copies. Many runtimes build a new string when you concatenate or replace, even if the source looked mutable in the prompt.
parts.why: Phone-screen questions hide cost inside string APIs. If you mutate by building a fresh buffer every time, a nested loop that looks linear becomes quadratic. Naming the copy turns a surprise timeout into a predictable plan.
parts.example: SAMPLE: you reverse the characters of "interview" in place inside a mutable array of chars, swapping ends toward the center. That stays linear. A different path that keeps writing s = s + nextChar inside a loop of length n allocates a new string each time and quietly pays a triangular sum of copies.
parts.use: Use string tools when the domain is text, tokens, or codepoints and the language gives you cheap indexing. Convert to a character array when you need true in-place swaps. Prefer builders or buffers when you assemble output from many pieces.
parts.refuse: Refuse repeated immutable concatenation in a hot loop. Refuse treating a string as a linked list of characters when you need O(1) jumps to an index. Refuse encoding tricks that hide surrogates if the prompt cares about user-visible length.

body:
Rule. Treat a string as a character sequence with array-like indexing, then ask whether an edit copies. Many runtimes build a new string when you concatenate or replace, even if the source looked mutable in the prompt.

Why it matters. Phone-screen questions hide cost inside string APIs. If you mutate by building a fresh buffer every time, a nested loop that looks linear becomes quadratic. Naming the copy turns a surprise timeout into a predictable plan.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: you reverse the characters of "interview" in place inside a mutable array of chars, swapping ends toward the center. That stays linear. A different path that keeps writing s = s + nextChar inside a loop of length n allocates a new string each time and quietly pays a triangular sum of copies.

When to use. Use string tools when the domain is text, tokens, or codepoints and the language gives you cheap indexing. Convert to a character array when you need true in-place swaps. Prefer builders or buffers when you assemble output from many pieces.

When to refuse. Refuse repeated immutable concatenation in a hot loop. Refuse treating a string as a linked list of characters when you need O(1) jumps to an index. Refuse encoding tricks that hide surrogates if the prompt cares about user-visible length.
